title: Rearming the world is squeezing out women’s safety
gist: Global military spending reached US$2.9 trillion in 2025 (up 41% in a decade) while gender-equality aid fell and no gender SDG target is on track; the author argues Australia's UN Security Council bid should put the Women, Peace and Security agenda at its centre.

insights.claim: Global military expenditure reached US$2.9 trillion in 2025, up 41% over the past decade, per SIPRI, while bilateral aid targeting gender equality fell 13% between 2023 and 2024.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Budget priorities are shifting from social and peace spending to defence; supportive for defence-budget trajectories.
insights.locator: According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute

insights.claim: Not a single UN SDG gender equality target is on track for 2030, one in three national gender-equality institutions has lost authority in two years, and 316 million women experienced intimate-partner physical or sexual violence in the past year.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Evidence of broad retreat on gender-related development outcomes.
insights.locator: The latest UN Women Gender Snapshot

insights.claim: Militarisation creates gendered circuits of violence and capital in which military expansion depends on invisible care labour while depleting the care and social infrastructure on which human security depends, so rearmament may weaken the foundations of resilient societies.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: A critical framing of defence build-ups that may shape advocacy and aid policy debates.

insights.claim: Backlash (organised resistance to gender-equality advances) is distinct from regression (actual deterioration of women's rights), and backlash does not inevitably produce regression, as seen in some democracies where opposition coexists with greater women's representation.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: A useful distinction for assessing political risk related to gender policy.
insights.locator: Backlash is not the same as regression

insights.claim: In Afghanistan and Myanmar women's rights have been systematically dismantled through patriarchal authoritarian consolidation; V-Dem data show dramatic declines in women's civil liberties in both, reflecting the link between autocratisation and eroding gender equality.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Autocratisation and gender repression move together, a country-risk indicator.

insights.claim: Women resist repression through symbols and organising, such as Myanmar protesters hanging htamein across streets to obstruct soldiers and Afghan women sustaining underground education and documenting abuses.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Civil-society resilience persists even under severe repression.
insights.quote: Women are not merely victims requiring protection. They are political actors defending democratic freedoms and imagining alternative futures.

insights.claim: Australia's campaign for a 2029-30 UN Security Council seat should make Women, Peace and Security central via three shifts: prevention before militarisation, support for women's movements and not only governments, and coalitions defending international norms.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Signals what policy positions advocates will push in Australia's bid.

insights.claim: The greatest threat to WPS is that militarised and exclusionary visions of security become normalised, leaving women's rights, democratic participation and human security expendable.
insights.speaker: Jacqui True
insights.so_what: Security framing is shifting toward hard power, with soft-security programmes at risk of defunding.
